02

Teaching Philosophy & Approach

Across six art history courses and nine semesters at the University of Central Florida, a consistent set of commitments shapes every syllabus: an inclusive, object-based approach to the canon; clear structure that still respects students as independent adults; writing and visual analysis as non-negotiable core skills; and a transparent, evolving stance on generative AI.

01
Inclusive, Global Surveys
Every survey course re-centers the canon toward the art and artists it has historically excluded — Indigenous America, African American art, and global modernisms sit alongside the European tradition, not after it. Co-authored the adopted textbook for American Art, This is America: Re-viewing the Art of the United States (Oxford University Press, 2023), built around this same principle.
02
Structured Independence
Fully online, asynchronous courses are built on a weekly rhythm — reading, quiz, discussion post, essay — with no penalty for working ahead and no weekly late penalty, paired with one firm end-of-term deadline. The design trusts students to manage their own pace while making the consequences of procrastination explicit from day one.
03
Writing & Visual Analysis as Core Skills
Every course requires regular, cited written responses (300–500 words) and peer-engaged discussion posts, not just recognition-based quizzes. Upper-division courses add exhibition reviews, evaluative reports, and a capstone research project — building toward independent scholarly writing.
04
Transparent, Evolving AI Policy
Course AI policies have shifted from a blanket restriction (2023–25) to a disclosed, assignment-by-assignment framework (2026) that requires students to cite exactly where and how GenAI was used — treating disclosure, not prohibition, as the operative academic-integrity standard as the technology and the field's norms mature.

"Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is governed on an assignment-by-assignment basis. … When using GenAI, you must disclose specifically where and how it was used in the process of completing the assignment. … Ultimately, students are responsible for the accuracy and veracity of submitted work whether AI-generated or not."

— AI Use Policy, ARH 2050 / ARH 3880 / ARH 4430 syllabi, Fall 2026

03

Courses Taught

Six original and adopted syllabi at the University of Central Florida's School of Visual Arts and Design, spanning the survey sequence through senior-level seminars. Select any course to view its full description, learning outcomes, and assessment structure.

ARH 2050 · Section 0061
History of Western Art I
Fall 2026 · Fully Online (WW) · 3 Credit Hours · General Education Program

Introduces visual culture — painting, sculpture, and architecture — in the European tradition from approximately 25,000 BCE to 1400 CE, from Prehistory through the Early Renaissance, covering the Ancient Near East, Egypt, Greece, Rome, Byzantium, the Middle Ages, and select art from Asia and Africa. The goal is to build familiarity with the core canon while understanding the intersections of the European tradition with global visual discourse.

Student Learning Outcomes
  • Question the continually changing category of experience that comprises the notion of art itself
  • Recognize a core group of images within the Western canon and interpret them within their socio-historical and cultural context
  • Develop skills of critical reading, visual analysis, and written expression
Assessment
Visual Art Analysis Exercises35%
Quizzes25%
Midterm20%
Final Exam20%
Text: Gardner's Art Through the Ages, 16th ed. (Kleiner) TA: Aisa Uchimura
ARH 3610 · Sections 0M01 & 0W60
American Art
Spring 2023 · Spring 2024 · Spring 2026 · Mixed-Mode & Fully Online · 3 Credit Hours

An inclusive introduction to American visual culture from early history to the present, relating art and artists to diverse social, political, and cultural contexts. The 2026 offering added a focus on how nationhood and identity are expressed through visual culture as institutions nationwide prepared for the United States' 250th anniversary. The 2023–24 mixed-mode sections gave students a weekly choice between in-person discussion and an online written response — a flexible, equity-minded participation structure.

Student Learning Outcomes
  • Identify and critically engage with the art and history of the United States
  • Appreciate the challenges inherent in studying art history and use art to connect past and present
  • Demonstrate discourse, analysis, and evaluation skills appropriate to art history
Assessment (2026, Fully Online)
Reading Response Essays40%
Discussion Posts30%
Quizzes15%
Final Exam15%
Text: This is America: Re-viewing the Art of the United States, Watson & Navaroli (Oxford UP, 2023) — instructor's own co-authored textbook

2023–24 mixed-mode assessment: Discussion/Class Participation 35% · Quizzes 30% · Exhibition Review Selection 5% · Exhibition Review 10% · Final Exam 20%.

ARH 3631 · Section 0M01
African-American Art
Spring 2025 · Mixed-Mode (In-Person Tuesdays + Online) · 3 Credit Hours

A historical survey of art produced by working artists of African heritage and representations of African American life, tracing how race relations in the United States have been reflected in painting, drawing, printmaking, sculpture, and public art. Each week, students choose between an in-person seminar discussion or a written online response and peer reply.

Student Learning Outcomes
  • Question the continually changing category of experience that comprises the notion of art
  • Recognize a core group of images by Black artists and interpret them within their socio-historical and cultural context
  • Develop skills of critical reading, visual analysis, and oral and written expression
Assessment
Discussion Board Posts40%
Quizzes40%
Final Essay20%
Text: African-American Art: A Visual and Cultural History, Lisa Farrington (Oxford UP, 2017)
ARH 3880 · Section 0061
History of Immersive Experience
Fall 2026 · Fully Online (WW) · 3 Credit Hours

Traces the history of immersive experience from late-eighteenth-century pleasure gardens to contemporary theme parks, analyzing the design and narrative theory behind the world's most famous themed spaces and situating them within the historical movements that shaped them.

Student Learning Outcomes
  • Outline the important historical sites, designers, and texts that have influenced immersive experience
  • Recognize the qualities of the built environment
  • Evaluate various types of immersive experiences and measure their effectiveness
  • Identify and discuss essential literature on the topic
Assessment
Discussion Board Posts50%
Quizzes35%
Final Evaluative Project15%

Sample weekly topics: Italian & French Gardens · Pleasure Gardens & Urban Parks · Dioramas, Panoramas & Cycloramas · World's Fairs · Stereographs, Kinetoscopes, VR & AR · Amusement & Theme Parks · Video Games · Contemporary Immersive Artists.

ARH 4430 · Sections 0W60 & 0061
19th Century Art
Fall 2025 · Fall 2026 · Fully Online (WW) · Senior-Level · 3 Credit Hours

A survey of the trends and developments in 19th-century art in America and Western Europe — a period of revolution — introducing the major artists, works, techniques, and styles of modernity within their cultural, political, and economic contexts.

Student Learning Outcomes
  • Question the continually changing category of experience that comprises the notion of art
  • Recognize a core group of images within 19th-century art and interpret them within their socio-historical and cultural context
  • Develop skills of critical reading, visual analysis, and oral and written expression
Assessment
Reading Response Essays40%
Discussion Posts30%
Quizzes15%
Final Exam15%
Text: Nineteenth-Century Art: A Critical History, Stephen Eisenman (Thames & Hudson)
ARH 4450 · Section 0W61
20th Century Art
Spring 2025 · Fully Online (WW) · Senior-Level · 3 Credit Hours

Introduces the history of modern art from the late nineteenth through the twentieth century, examining art's role in the development of modern culture and its relationship to socio-political transformation — from the historic avant-gardes and the rise of abstraction through postwar neo-avant-garde practices and 1980s–90s postmodernism. No assigned textbook: readings are drawn from scholarly essays, book chapters, and digital exhibitions curated specifically for the course.

Student Learning Outcomes
  • Broaden and deepen understanding of specific artists, movements, strategies, and practices of the twentieth century
  • Deepen skills at critical reading and analysis of modern art within historical and theoretical context
  • Strengthen ability to discuss, debate, and articulate the artistic, social, and political stakes of modern practices
  • Hone research and writing through reading responses, two exams, and a 6–7 page final research project
  • Develop verbal communication and professional presentation through class discussion
Assessment
Weekly Reading Responses & Discussion60%
Midterm Exam20%
Final Exam20%
